overture.name: Overture Maps Foundation — Places

more_links.label: Places theme: sources, licenses and monthly releases

overture.licence: Varies by contributor: CDLA-Permissive-2.0, Apache 2.0 or CC0 1.0
overture.credit: Source: Overture Maps Foundation, overturemaps.org, Places theme, release 2026-09-23.1, accessed 1 October 2026 (Meta, Microsoft, Foursquare, AllThePlaces and others). Foursquare records: © Foursquare Labs, Inc., Apache License 2.0, transformed to the Overture schema
overture.access: The overturemaps command-line tool downloads the Places theme from Overture's public cloud-hosted files, cut to a box around Puerto Rico (west -67.97, south 17.85, east -65.20, north 18.57). The current snapshot is Overture release 2026-09-23.1, downloaded on 1 October 2026.
overture.cadence: Overture releases the Places theme every month. The observatory keeps one snapshot and renews it only when FPR rebuilds the data (a new snapshot).
overture.used_for: Every tourism place on the maps (name, category, location, address, website, confidence score and source dataset) and every count, density and exposure figure built from those places. Also the road distance from where residents live to the nearest supermarket, food store, pharmacy and bank or cooperativa, by barrio and municipio (essentials_series.json, essentials_barrio.json; only the distances, never the shops). Also, to spread each municipio's jobs over its business places in the estimate of jobs within reach (jobs_reach_series.json; no place is published).
overture.terms_note: The license depends on who contributed the record: CDLA-Permissive-2.0 for Meta, Microsoft and others, Apache 2.0 for Foursquare and CC0 1.0 for AllThePlaces. In the 2026-10 snapshot the observatory publishes 32,541 places. The listed source is Meta for 31,945, Foursquare for 252, Microsoft for 241 and AllThePlaces for 103. Overture's other themes (Buildings, Divisions, Transportation) use ODbL; the observatory also uses Buildings, under its own source card (overture_buildings). Overture suggests citing 'Overture Maps Foundation, overturemaps.org' with the access date. Foursquare's notice asks anyone who uses its records to keep attribution to Foursquare (including the full text of its NOTICE.txt), to give recipients a copy of the Apache 2.0 license and to mark any changes; Overture's attribution page carries Foursquare's copyright line. Listings are third-party business records, not an official register. FPR classifies and de-duplicates them. Phone numbers, emails and social-media links are not published.

fcc_bdc.name: FCC — Broadband Data Collection, fixed broadband availability (National Broadband Map)
fcc_bdc.publisher: Federal Communications Commission (FCC), Broadband Data Task Force

more_links.label: BDC help center: data specifications and the public data API (an FCC account and API token are needed)
NTIA, BEAD program: served, underserved and unserved

fcc_bdc.credit: Source: FCC Broadband Data Collection, fixed broadband availability data, as of June 30 of each year (https://broadbandmap.fcc.gov/)
fcc_bdc.access: The FCC's public data API answers only with an account: the build reads FPR's FCC username and API token from the GitHub Actions secrets FCC_BDC_USERNAME and FCC_BDC_HASH and sends them only to broadbandmap.fcc.gov. It downloads Puerto Rico's state location files (one CSV per fixed technology, about 60 MB a release), keeps counts by census block in its cache, and publishes only counts and shares by area. The site never calls the FCC.
fcc_bdc.cadence: Providers file twice a year, as of June 30 and December 31; the FCC publishes each release a few months later and again as challenges are settled. The observatory keeps the June release of each year and checks for a new one every 30 days (refresh unit broadband).
fcc_bdc.used_for: Broadband serviceable locations, the shares served, underserved and unserved in NTIA's BEAD terms, the locations below 100/20 Mbps and the share where fiber is available, for the 78 municipios, the 901 barrios and Puerto Rico, June 2023-2026 (broadband_series.json, broadband_barrio.json).
fcc_bdc.terms_note: Works of the US Government are not protected by US copyright. The location list behind the files (the Fabric) is licensed by CostQuest Associates and is not used: the public files give each location's census block, and the observatory publishes no location id, address or provider list. Availability is what providers report and can be challenged.

overture_buildings.name: Overture Maps Foundation — Buildings
overture_buildings.publisher: Overture Maps Foundation (OpenStreetMap contributors, Google Open Buildings, Microsoft ML Buildings and others)
overture_buildings.credit: © OpenStreetMap contributors, Overture Maps Foundation (overturemaps.org), Buildings theme, release 2026-10-21.0, ODbL 1.0
overture_buildings.access: The overturemaps package reads the Buildings theme from Overture's public GeoParquet files for a box around Puerto Rico (west -67.97, south 17.85, east -65.20, north 18.57), about 3.5 minutes. The build keeps, for each building, one point inside its outline, its footprint area, its first source and its height (cache/buildings/, not published). The site never calls Overture.
overture_buildings.cadence: Overture releases every month; the refresh checks every 30 days and rebuilds with the newest release (refresh unit buildings).
overture_buildings.used_for: The number of buildings, buildings per km², the land under roofs, the median footprint, the buildings in a FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area and the share traced by machine learning, for the 78 municipios, the 901 barrios and Puerto Rico (buildings_series.json, buildings_barrio.json).
overture_buildings.terms_note: ODbL 1.0 because the theme holds OpenStreetMap data: attribution as above, and share-alike for a derived database. The observatory's buildings files are counts and shares derived from it, so they are offered under ODbL 1.0 too. In release 2026-10-21.0, Puerto Rico's 2,157,363 buildings come from OpenStreetMap (1,500,399), Google Open Buildings (536,571) and Microsoft ML Buildings (120,393); 203,060 have a height. Footprints traced by machine learning can include sheds and miss buildings under trees. Most buildings are homes: nothing is published per building.

nasa_firms.name: NASA FIRMS — VIIRS 375 m active fire detections (NOAA-20)
nasa_firms.publisher: NASA Land, Atmosphere Near real-time Capability for EOS (LANCE), Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS)

more_links.label: FIRMS frequently asked questions (what a detection is, credit)

nasa_firms.licence: NASA open data, no restriction on use
nasa_firms.credit: NASA FIRMS (LANCE), VIIRS 375 m active fire detections, NOAA-20
nasa_firms.access: The build downloads FIRMS's yearly country files for Puerto Rico (NOAA-20, standard processing; public, no key) and, in GitHub Actions only, the last 12 months from the FIRMS area API for the Puerto Rico box with FPR's MAP_KEY, kept as the secret FIRMS_MAP_KEY. The detections stay in the build's cache; only counts by municipio are published. The site never calls FIRMS.
nasa_firms.cadence: FIRMS adds detections within hours of each pass; the yearly file of a finished year appears in the first months of the next. The observatory rebuilds monthly (refresh unit fires).
nasa_firms.used_for: Vegetation fire detections by municipio for each year since 2019, per 100 km² of land, and in the last 12 months (fires_series.json).
nasa_firms.terms_note: NASA's data are open with no restriction; FIRMS asks that published work credit 'NASA FIRMS'. A detection is a 375 m pixel that held one or more fires or other heat sources when the satellite passed, not a fire's outline or size. Suomi NPP stopped sending FIRMS data on 2026-11-02, so the observatory uses NOAA-20 for every year.

fema_nfhl.name: FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer (NFHL)

more_links.label: Data service used by the build (for developers)
NFHL metadata: constraints and update frequency

fema_nfhl.licence: US Government work; FEMA's metadata lists no access constraints
fema_nfhl.credit: Source: FEMA, National Flood Hazard Layer (NFHL)
fema_nfhl.access: ArcGIS REST service (a public web service that returns map data on request) on hazards.fema.gov: NFHL MapServer, layer 28, Flood Hazard Zones. The build pages through the layer with the filter DFIRM_ID LIKE '72%' (Puerto Rico) and reads the fields FLD_ZONE, ZONE_SUBTY, SFHA_TF and STATIC_BFE. No key is needed.
fema_nfhl.cadence: FEMA says it adds new and revised data continuously, and its metadata gives a monthly update frequency. The observatory keeps one snapshot, downloaded on 1 October 2026, and renews it only when FPR rebuilds the data (a new snapshot).
fema_nfhl.used_for: The flood zone shapes on the maps (flood.geojson) and the flood-zone flags and shares for tourism places and municipalities. Also the roads that close in the estimate of residents cut off from hospitals by floods (cutoff_series.json, cutoff_barrio.json).
fema_nfhl.terms_note: FEMA's metadata says the printed Flood Insurance Rate Map, its database and the Flood Insurance Study are the official designation of Special Flood Hazard Areas and base flood elevations. The observatory draws a simplified copy for context. It is not a flood determination for any property.

padus.name: USGS — PAD-US 4.1 (protected areas)
padus.publisher: US Geological Survey (USGS), Gap Analysis Project

more_links.label: Data service used by the build (for developers)

padus.credit: Source: U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) Gap Analysis Project (GAP), 2024, Protected Areas Database of the United States (PAD-US) 4.1: U.S. Geological Survey data release, https://doi.org/10.5066/P96WBCHS
padus.access: ArcGIS REST FeatureServer layer 0 (a public web service) of a hosted copy of PAD-US 4.1 (layer PADUS4_1ProtMechCat, service Protection_Mechanism_Category_PADUS, on a USGS ArcGIS Online account). The build pages through it with the filter State_Nm='PR' and reads Unit_Nm, Mang_Name, Des_Tp, GAP_Sts, Category, Pub_Access and GIS_Acres. No key is needed.
padus.cadence: USGS publishes PAD-US in numbered versions. As of 3 October 2026 it lists version 4.1 (released March 2025, cited by USGS as a 2024 data release) as the most recent. The observatory keeps one snapshot, downloaded on 1 October 2026, and renews it only when FPR rebuilds the data (a new snapshot).
padus.used_for: The protected-area outlines on the maps (protected.geojson), the protected-area name and status for each tourism place, and the share of places inside protected areas.
padus.terms_note: USGS says its data are in the US public domain, and USGS and its data partners disclaim liability for misuse. PAD-US combines data from federal, state and local agencies and nonprofit partners. USGS recommends it for comparing agencies and advises asking the managing agency directly for authoritative boundaries. Proclamation boundaries (designation type PROC) are drawn but do not count a place as inside a protected area. The observatory draws a simplified copy.

census_tiger.name: US Census Bureau — TIGERweb boundaries and counts

more_links.label: 2020 Census county subdivisions, the barrios (layer 20, full resolution)

census_tiger.credit: Source: US Census Bureau, TIGERweb (2010 and 2020 Census counts, 2020 Census blocks, 2023 generalized boundaries)
census_tiger.access: ArcGIS REST services (public web services that return map data on request) on tigerweb.geo.census.gov, no key, always filtered to STATE='72'. 2020 Census Counties (layer 82) give each municipio's population, housing units and area. Generalized_ACS2023 Counties 500K (layer 11) give the shoreline-clipped boundaries drawn on the maps. 2010 Census Counties (layer 100) give 2010 population. 2020 Census Blocks (layer 10) give block population. Generalized_ACS2023 County Subdivisions 500K (layer 7) give barrio outlines. 2020 Census Tracts (layer 6), Block Groups (layer 8) and County Subdivisions (layer 20) give each unit's name, land area, residents and housing units; the county subdivision outlines at full resolution place each census block in its barrio (geo.py). Layer 10 also gives each block's 15-digit id, housing units and land area.
census_tiger.cadence: The Census Bureau issues these layers by vintage (the 2010 and 2020 censuses, and 2023 generalized boundaries), so they do not change between vintages. The observatory keeps one snapshot, downloaded on 1 October 2026 (the tract, block group and county subdivision tables and the block ids on 6 October 2026), and renews it only when FPR rebuilds the data (a new snapshot).
census_tiger.used_for: Municipality and barrio boundaries, the 2010 and 2020 population and housing-unit counts per municipality, the block population behind the transit coverage figures, and the municipality of each place and stop. The 2020 geography crosswalk (units, parents, residents and housing units of each unit, barrio-to-tract weights) and the block ids and housing units behind it.
census_tiger.terms_note: The Census Bureau's TIGER/Line technical documentation says copyright protection is not available for works of the US Government and asks users to cite the Census Bureau as the source. The Bureau's citation page adds that conclusions drawn from any analysis of the data are the sole responsibility of the performing party. FPR's use of these data is not endorsed by the Census Bureau. The 2020 layer's legal boundaries include coastal water (they reach 3 nautical miles out), so the maps and point lookups use the shoreline-clipped generalized boundaries instead. Barrios are Census county subdivisions. The observatory does not use parcel (catastro) data from CRIM, the Centro de Recaudación de Ingresos Municipales (Municipal Revenue Collection Center).

census_cartographic.name: US Census Bureau — Cartographic boundary files, 2020 (1:500,000)
census_cartographic.licence: No license stated on the product pages; US Government work
census_cartographic.credit: Source: US Census Bureau, cartographic boundary files (2020 Census tracts and block groups, 1:500,000)
census_cartographic.access: Two zip files of shapefiles on www2.census.gov/geo/tiger/GENZ2020/shp, no key: cb_2020_72_tract_500k.zip (0.6 MB) and cb_2020_72_bg_500k.zip (1.0 MB), last modified 19 May 2023 and read on 6 October 2026. geo.py reads them with pyshp and writes site/data/geo/tracts.geojson and blockgroups.geojson, keeping only the GEOID.
census_cartographic.cadence: A 2020 geography. The files are not revised within a decade except to correct errors. The observatory downloads them once and does not refresh them unless the build is run with its refresh option.
census_cartographic.used_for: The outlines of census tracts and block groups, for drawing only.
census_cartographic.terms_note: The Census Bureau describes these files as simplified representations designed for small-scale thematic mapping and says on its description page: "These files should not be used for: geographic analysis including area or perimeter calculation." The observatory uses them only to draw outlines; land areas come from the Census Bureau's own land-area field (AREALAND) and counts from the 2020 block table. The generalized files are clipped to a simplified outline of the coast and "some offshore areas may be excluded", so the 42 tracts and 42 block groups that are all water have no outline. The description page states no copyright or citation rule. The TIGER/Line documentation, which covers a related product, says copyright protection is not available for works of the US Government and asks users to cite the Census Bureau as the source. FPR's use of these files is not endorsed by the Census Bureau.

census_pep.name: US Census Bureau — Population Estimates (municipios)
census_pep.publisher: US Census Bureau, Population Estimates Program

more_links.label: Vintage 2025 age and sex, Puerto Rico (CSV)
Vintage 2025 state totals, Puerto Rico included (CSV)

census_pep.licence: US Government work; cite the Census Bureau as the source
census_pep.credit: Source: US Census Bureau, Population Estimates Program (Vintage 2020 for 2010-2019, Vintage 2025 for 2020-2025)
census_pep.access: Public CSV files on www2.census.gov, no key: PRM-EST2020.csv (totals) and PRM-EST2020-AGESEX.csv for 2010-2019 (Vintage 2020), and cc-est2025-agesex-72.csv for 2020-2025 (Vintage 2025). gii.py reads Puerto Rico's row of the newest state totals file (NST-EST2025-ALLDATA.csv) and keeps it in cache/gii/.
census_pep.cadence: The Census Bureau issues a new vintage every year (Vintage 2025 appeared in June 2026) and says the latest vintage replaces earlier estimates for the same dates. The observatory reads the newest vintage that has a Puerto Rico file when FPR rebuilds the data (a new snapshot).
census_pep.used_for: Resident population by municipality and the share of residents aged 65 and over, 2010 to 2025 in the 2026-10 snapshot (housing_series.json), shown on the Housing page and the Analysis tab; and Puerto Rico's population, the denominator of the FPR estimate of electricity output per million people (indicator 3.2.1 of the Global Innovation Index page, gii_profile.json). Also the 2010 and 2020 census counts by municipio, age and sex (the census bases of PRM-EST2020-AGESEX and CC-EST2025-AGESEX-72) and the island's births and deaths 2010-2020, for the estimate of net migration by age (netmig_age_series.json).
census_pep.terms_note: Estimates are for July 1. The 2010 and 2020 values are census counts for April 1. Estimates for 2011 to 2019 were built on the 2010 census and were not revised to the 2020 count, so the series jumps at 2020. The product pages state no license. The Census Bureau's TIGER/Line documentation, which covers a different product, says copyright protection is not available for works of the US Government. The Bureau's citation page asks users to cite it as the source and says conclusions drawn from any analysis of the data are the sole responsibility of the performing party. FPR's use of these data is not endorsed by the Census Bureau.

census_decennial.name: US Census Bureau — 2010 and 2020 Census housing occupancy
census_decennial.licence: US Government work; cite the Census Bureau as the source
census_decennial.credit: Source: US Census Bureau, 2010 and 2020 Census, PL 94-171 Redistricting Data (table H1, housing occupancy)
census_decennial.access: Two public ZIP files on www2.census.gov, no key: census_2010/01-Redistricting_File--PL_94-171/Puerto_Rico/pr2010.pl.zip and programs-surveys/decennial/2020/data/01-Redistricting_File--PL_94-171/Puerto_Rico/pr2020.pl.zip. The build reads each file's place-code table and the part that holds table H1 (housing occupancy), and keeps the island total and the 78 municipios.
census_decennial.cadence: A census is taken every ten years, on April 1 (2010 and 2020; the next is 2030), so these files do not change. The observatory reads them once and keeps the result.
census_decennial.used_for: Housing units, vacant units, vacancy rate and residents per housing unit on census day in 2010 and 2020 (housing_series.json).
census_decennial.terms_note: Census-day vacancy counts and American Community Survey vacancy estimates measure vacancy differently, so compare each source only with itself. The product pages state no license. The Census Bureau's TIGER/Line documentation, which covers a different product, says copyright protection is not available for works of the US Government. The Bureau's citation page asks users to cite it as the source and says conclusions drawn from any analysis of the data are the sole responsibility of the performing party. FPR's use of these data is not endorsed by the Census Bureau.

acs5.name: US Census Bureau — American Community Survey 5-year
acs5.publisher: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey

more_links.label: Accuracy of the Data (margins of error)

acs5.licence: US Government work; cite the Census Bureau as the source
acs5.credit: Source: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, 2006-2010 through 2020-2024
acs5.access: Public summary files on www2.census.gov, no key. For the 2010 to 2020 vintages: per-sequence files under 5_year_seq_by_state/PuertoRico (and the 2012 Puerto Rico ZIP used for the 2008-2012 baseline). For 2021 to 2024: table-based files named acsdt5y{year}-{table}.dat. The build keeps the island and its 78 municipios. A second reader, acs_small.py, reads the tract, block group and barrio rows of the 2021 to 2024 table-based files by byte ranges (all five levels of a table cost 0.5 to 1.5 MB, against 18 to 121 MB for the nationwide file). small_area.py builds from it the files of barrios, census tracts and block groups (acs_barrio.json, acs_tract.json, acs_blockgroup.json) and the Population domain's series (population_series.json). The build also reads the Census Bureau's keyless table definitions at api.census.gov (the cell labels of each table, https://api.census.gov/data/{year}/acs/acs5/groups/{table}.json) to check that the cells it uses are the ones it means; no page of the site calls that host.
acs5.cadence: The Census Bureau releases a new 5-year vintage every year. In the 2026-10 snapshot the newest window the observatory holds is 2020-2024. The build checks for a newer table-based file and adds it when FPR rebuilds the data (a new snapshot).
acs5.used_for: Municipality housing, income, poverty, employment, education, cost-burden, commuting, vehicle and internet variables (housing_series.json and economy_series.json), plus the 2008-2012 baseline and the affordability figures. For 2021 to 2024, the same variables and the age, household, veteran and disability shares for 901 barrios, 981 census tracts and 2,555 block groups, with their margins of error. The age bands and age groups (population_age.json; the shares of the age groups also in population_series.json and, for 18 to 44 and 45 to 64, the barrio and tract files), from B01001 and B09001. Women's and men's labor force participation, unemployment and the counts behind them by sex and age group, for the 78 municipios and any group of them, in the three windows that share no year (2010-2014, 2015-2019, 2020-2024), from B23001, B23003, B98003 and B98001 (labor_sex_series.json and women_labor.json, women_labor.py).
acs5.terms_note: These are survey estimates. Each pools 60 months of answers, and the Census Bureau publishes margins of error at a 90 percent confidence level (see its 'Accuracy of the Data' document), which the observatory keeps where they exist. Windows are labelled by their last year. Dollar values are in the dollars of that last year, not adjusted for inflation. The product pages state no license. The Census Bureau's TIGER/Line documentation, which covers a different product, says copyright protection is not available for works of the US Government. The Bureau's citation page asks users to cite it as the source and says conclusions drawn from any analysis of the data are the sole responsibility of the performing party. FPR's use of these data is not endorsed by the Census Bureau.

more_links.label: Public Assistance Funded Projects Details, v2
Housing Assistance Program Data, Owners, v2
Housing Assistance Program Data, Renters, v2

openfema.credit: Source: Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), OpenFEMA API v2 (https://www.fema.gov/api/open/v2/): Housing Assistance Program Data (Owners and Renters) and Disaster Declarations Summaries, retrieved 2 October 2026; Public Assistance Funded Projects Details and HMA Subapplications, retrieved 30 October 2026. This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA. openfema.access: OpenFEMA API, version 2 (https://www.fema.gov/api/open/v2/), no key, read 1,000 rows at a time: HousingAssistanceOwners and HousingAssistanceRenters (state eq 'PR'), DisasterDeclarationsSummaries (used to date each disaster), PublicAssistanceFundedProjectsDetails (stateNumberCode eq '72') and HmaSubapplications (subapplicantStateAbbreviation eq 'PR').
openfema.cadence: FEMA refreshes its housing and public assistance datasets daily, and the declarations about every 20 minutes. The observatory reads them only when FPR rebuilds the data (a new snapshot) and keeps a copy between rebuilds, so its figures can differ from FEMA's current data.
openfema.used_for: FEMA Individual Assistance households and dollars by municipality and declaration year (housing_series.json) and FEMA Public Assistance obligations by municipality, in total and by damage category, and FEMA Hazard Mitigation Assistance approved, obligated and awaiting decision by benefiting municipality (economy_series.json).
openfema.terms_note: OpenFEMA's terms ask users to name the endpoint (with its version) and the date and time the data were retrieved. They also ask users to include this statement: 'This product uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's OpenFEMA API, but is not endorsed by FEMA. The Federal Government or FEMA cannot vouch for the data or analyses derived from these data after the data have been retrieved from the Agency's website(s).' The terms limit use to statistical research or as a reporting record, bar re-identifying people, and bar using the data to decide anyone's eligibility for benefits. FEMA says the housing and project figures come from its case systems, not its official financial systems, and can differ slightly from USAspending. Housing records are aggregated and non-personal. A large part of Public Assistance is recorded as statewide and cannot be placed in a municipality: in the 2026-10 snapshot, the statewide share of each declaration year's obligations ranges from 11% (2010) to 88% (2009).

lineage.en: FEMA's own project and subapplication records. Authoritative for Public Assistance and Hazard Mitigation dollars by applicant or benefiting municipio; COR3 and USAspending report the same obligations and are never added to them.

hrsa_sites.name: HRSA — Health Center Service Delivery and Look-Alike Sites
hrsa_sites.publisher: Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), Bureau of Primary Health Care

more_links.label: The file the build reads (CSV, all states; for developers)

hrsa_sites.licence: CC0 1.0 (public domain) as Data.gov lists this file (its Excel version); HRSA's download page lists no usage limitations. Treated as open; HRSA has not confirmed the terms
hrsa_sites.credit: Source: US Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), Data Warehouse, Health Center Service Delivery and Look-Alike Sites, downloaded 6 October 2026
hrsa_sites.access: Direct download of one CSV file from data.hrsa.gov (all states and territories); no key. The build streams the file, keeps the Puerto Rico rows (Site State Abbreviation = PR) and only seven columns (status, type, location type, county code, state, record date), and drops names, addresses, telephone numbers, web addresses and coordinates before anything is written to disk.
hrsa_sites.cadence: HRSA says it refreshes the file daily. The observatory keeps one snapshot (6 October 2026) and renews it only when FPR rebuilds the data (python health_series.py).
hrsa_sites.used_for: Counts of permanent health center sites and of mobile vans in each municipality (health_series.json: hc_sites, hc_vans).
hrsa_sites.terms_note: HRSA's download page lists "Usage limitations: None" for this file. Data.gov's record for it gives the license as CC0 1.0 ("No rights reserved. This data is in the public domain.") but lists only the Excel version of the file; the build reads the CSV. Data.gov's record for the HRSA Data Warehouse as a whole names the Open Database License 1.0 (credit and share-alike) and says its portal offers downloadable data files on health center sites, so the same doubt as for the shortage-area files applies. The observatory treats the file as open, credits HRSA in the dataset window, the data dictionary and the About tab, and HANDOFF decision 38 asks the owner whether to ask HRSA to confirm the terms in writing. It publishes counts for each municipality only and never names, addresses, telephone numbers, web addresses or coordinates.

hrsa_hpsa.name: HRSA — Health Professional Shortage Area (HPSA) designations
hrsa_hpsa.publisher: Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), Bureau of Health Workforce, Division of Policy and Shortage Designation

more_links.label: Designated HPSA Quarterly Summary (the national and state totals the build was checked against)
HRSA's shortage designation criteria and scoring
The files the build reads (CSV, all states; for developers): primary care

hrsa_hpsa.licence: CC0 1.0 (public domain) as Data.gov lists these files, whose record also says "restricted public"; HRSA's download page lists no usage limitations. Treated as open; HRSA has not confirmed the terms
hrsa_hpsa.credit: Source: US Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), Data Warehouse, Health Professional Shortage Area designations (primary care, dental health, mental health), downloaded 6 October 2026
hrsa_hpsa.access: Direct download of three CSV files from data.hrsa.gov (one for each discipline, all states and territories); no key. The build streams each file, keeps the Puerto Rico rows (Primary State or Common State = PR) and sixteen columns (status, designation type, score, practitioners in place and needed, population, county code and the like), and drops the names of the designations before anything is written to disk.
hrsa_hpsa.cadence: HRSA says it refreshes the files daily; designations change when HRSA reviews them and when withdrawals are published in the Federal Register, generally once a year. The observatory keeps one snapshot (6 October 2026) and renews it only when FPR rebuilds the data (python health_series.py).
hrsa_hpsa.used_for: Priority score, practitioners still needed and share of need met of the area-level shortage designations in each municipality, for primary care, dental health and mental health (health_series.json).
hrsa_hpsa.terms_note: HRSA's download page lists "Usage limitations: None" for these files. Data.gov's record for the Shortage Designation Management System (published by HRSA's Bureau of Health Workforce; a file entry is dated 3 September 2026 and Data.gov last crawled the record on 28 September 2026) lists the three files and gives the license as CC0 1.0 and the rights statement "No rights reserved. This data is in the public domain." It also sets the access level "restricted public" (the federal metadata schema defines it as "available under certain use restrictions") and marks every file "Restricted - Partly": the record contradicts itself, which is why the source is marked link-works-licence-unclear. Data.gov's record for the HRSA Data Warehouse as a whole (modified 26 July 2023, last crawled 10 September 2026) names the Open Database License 1.0, which asks for credit and share-alike, and says the portal offers downloadable data files on health center sites and shortage areas, so it may cover these files too: if it applied, the credit line would need to say so. The observatory treats the files as open, credits HRSA in the dataset window, the data dictionary and the About tab, and HANDOFF decision 38 asks the owner whether to ask HRSA to confirm the terms in writing. The observatory publishes counts for each municipality only and never names, addresses, telephone numbers, web addresses or coordinates. HRSA warns that its formulas count certain practitioners only: primary care physicians (not nurse practitioners or physician assistants), dentists, and, for every mental health designation of Puerto Rico, psychiatrists (not psychologists, social workers or other providers).

bls_qcew.name: BLS — Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW)
bls_qcew.credit: Source: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW)
bls_qcew.access: QCEW open-data CSV files, no key: https://data.bls.gov/cew/data/api/{year}/a/area/{area}.csv for each of the 78 municipio areas and for Puerto Rico (area 72000), annual averages. The build also tests whether the next year's file exists.
bls_qcew.cadence: BLS publishes QCEW every quarter and posts annual averages after the year ends. As of 28 August 2026 the latest release covered the first quarter of 2026; the second quarter is due 2 December 2026. In the 2026-10 snapshot the observatory holds 2014 to 2025. It re-reads the files when FPR rebuilds the data (a new snapshot).
bls_qcew.used_for: Jobs, establishments, wages, jobs by industry, tourism-related jobs and industry concentration by municipality and year (economy_series.json). Also the jobs of the estimate of jobs within reach by car (jobs_reach_series.json).
bls_qcew.terms_note: BLS says everything it publishes is in the public domain and asks users to cite it as the source. Cells that would identify one employer are withheld, and the observatory leaves them blank, so small municipalities miss many industries. Jobs are counted where the work is done. BLS says QCEW covers more than 95 percent of US jobs. The observatory does not measure that share for Puerto Rico. QCEW leaves out unincorporated self-employed workers, unpaid family workers and some other groups.

bls_laus.name: BLS — Local Area Unemployment Statistics (LAUS)
bls_laus.credit: Source: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Local Area Unemployment Statistics (LAUS), retrieved through the BLS Public Data API on 3 October 2026. BLS.gov cannot vouch for the data or analyses derived from these data after the data have been retrieved from BLS.gov.
bls_laus.access: BLS Public Data API, version 1 (https://api.bls.gov/publicAPI/v1/timeseries/data/), no key, POST requests for annual averages: municipio series LAUCN72xxx0000000003 (unemployment rate) and LAUCN72xxx0000000006 (labor force), and the Puerto Rico series LASST72. BLS limits the keyless version of the API to 25 queries a day.
bls_laus.cadence: BLS publishes LAUS every month and an annual average after year end. In the 2026-10 snapshot the observatory holds 2010 to 2025, with no value for 2020 because BLS's file has no annual average for that year. The latest year (2025) is preliminary. The observatory re-reads the series when FPR rebuilds the data (a new snapshot).
bls_laus.used_for: Unemployment rate, labor force, employed and unemployed residents by municipality and year (economy_series.json). Puerto Rico's employment (LAUST720000000000005, annual average of the 12 months) in the FPR estimate of indicator 6.2.1 of the Global Innovation Index page (gii_profile.json).
bls_laus.terms_note: BLS says everything it publishes is in the public domain and asks users to cite it as the source. BLS's API terms require users to state that 'BLS.gov cannot vouch for the data or analyses derived from these data after the data have been retrieved from BLS.gov' and to cite the date the data were retrieved. BLS describes county estimates as built from employment and claims data and controlled to state totals. FPR found no BLS description of how municipio estimates are made for Puerto Rico. Estimates for small municipios can swing from year to year and can be revised.

bls_cpi.name: BLS — Consumer Price Index (CPI-U, US city average)
bls_cpi.credit: Source: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U), US city average, retrieved through the BLS Public Data API on 3 October 2026 (2010 to 2025) and 4 October 2026 (2000 to 2009). BLS.gov cannot vouch for the data or analyses derived from these data after the data have been retrieved from BLS.gov.
bls_cpi.access: BLS Public Data API, version 1 (https://api.bls.gov/publicAPI/v1/timeseries/data/), no key, one series: CUUR0000SA0 (CPI-U, US city average, all items), annual averages from 2000.
bls_cpi.cadence: BLS publishes the CPI every month. In the 2026-10 snapshot the observatory holds annual averages for 2000 to 2025. It re-reads them when FPR rebuilds the data (a new snapshot).
bls_cpi.used_for: Putting dollar amounts from different years on one footing. When a visitor ticks 'inflation-adjusted' on a dollar layer on the Analysis tab, amounts are restated in the dollars of the newest CPI year (2025 in the 2026-10 snapshot). The series starts in 2000, so the earliest FEMA declaration years (from 2001) can be adjusted too.
bls_cpi.terms_note: BLS says everything it publishes is in the public domain and asks users to cite it as the source. The index covers the US city average, not Puerto Rico, so it only approximates price changes on the island. The index base is 1982-84 = 100. BLS's API terms require users to state that 'BLS.gov cannot vouch for the data or analyses derived from these data after the data have been retrieved from BLS.gov' and to cite the date the data were retrieved.

usaspending.name: USAspending.gov — federal awards by place of performance
usaspending.licence: No license stated for the data (the API's source code is CC0-1.0)

short.es: USAspending.gov

usaspending.credit: Source: USAspending.gov, US Department of the Treasury, federal awards by place of performance
usaspending.access: USAspending API (https://api.usaspending.gov/api/v2/search/spending_by_geography/), no key. For each federal fiscal year and award type the build sends two POST requests, both with scope place_of_performance and with subawards left out: one at the county layer for the 78 municipios, and one at the state layer with the code PR for the Puerto Rico total. For the seven assistance listings mapped on their own (96.002, 96.001, 96.004, 64.109, 84.063, 93.600, 14.195) the same two requests are sent for each listing and fiscal year with a program_numbers filter instead of the award types (first downloaded 2026-10-31).
usaspending.cadence: USAspending.gov says new or updated data appear the day after an agency submits them. In the 2026-10 snapshot the observatory holds fiscal years 2008 to 2025. It counts a fiscal year as final from 15 November, about six weeks after it ends. It re-reads the data only when FPR rebuilds the data (a new snapshot), so values for earlier years can differ from what USAspending.gov shows later.
usaspending.used_for: Federal contracts, grants, direct payments, loans and other assistance by municipality and fiscal year, and a Puerto Rico total; obligations of seven assistance listings that are placed across the municipalities (Social Security retirement, disability and survivors benefits, veterans disability compensation, Pell Grants, Head Start, Project-Based Rental Assistance) (economy_series.json).
usaspending.terms_note: Amounts are obligations by federal fiscal year (October to September), not money spent. Place of performance is as the awarding agency reports it. Awards to the Commonwealth for statewide programs are often attributed to San Juan, so San Juan is overstated and other municipalities understated. The Puerto Rico total is USAspending's own total for the territory. It also counts awards that name no municipality, so the 78 municipalities add up to less than the island. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the share of the Puerto Rico total that names no municipality is between 3.4% (fiscal year 2011) and 24.7% (fiscal year 2024); the dataset dialog on the Analysis tab lists it by year. The USAspending.gov API documentation states no license for the data. Checked again on 2026-10-19 for the Data management page: usaspending.gov states no terms for the data on its pages; the Data.gov record of USAspending's raw files says "No license information was provided", and GAO-19-72 found that the website does not provide comprehensive licensing information for the data. So the class stays unstated; the Treasury would have to state the terms.

lineage.en: Federal awards as agencies report them to USAspending (DATA Act). Obligations by place of performance. FEMA Public Assistance, Hazard Mitigation and CDBG-DR prime awards land in San Juan here; for those, OpenFEMA and Vivienda are the sources that are added up (spending.py DEDUP_GROUPS).

noaa_slr.name: NOAA — Sea Level Rise Viewer

more_links.label: Digital Coast: sea level rise data page
Data service used by the build (for developers)
Sea level rise vector data download page (Puerto Rico)
Puerto Rico inundation and low-lying polygons, 0 to 10 ft (PR_slr_data_dist.zip, 23 MB)

noaa_slr.licence: No license stated; NOAA's disclaimer applies

short.es: visor de aumento del nivel del mar de NOAA

noaa_slr.credit: Source: NOAA Office for Coastal Management, Sea Level Rise Viewer
noaa_slr.access: Map tiles streamed live from NOAA's ArcGIS server to the visitor's browser: https://coast.noaa.gov/arcgis/rest/services/dc_slr/slr_{n}ft/MapServer/tile/{z}/{y}/{x}, with n from 1 to 10 feet. No key.  For the exposure series, exposure.py also downloads NOAA's polygon version of the same data once (a File Geodatabase, PR_slr_final_dist.gdb in PR_slr_data_dist.zip, 23 MB, dated 27 September 2023), reads the layers PR_slr_{n}ft (inundation connected to the ocean) and PR_low_{n}ft (low-lying areas not connected to it) for n from 1 to 10 feet, and keeps only counts of residents and housing units for each area, not the polygons.
noaa_slr.cadence: NOAA lists a 2022 and a 2017 scenario set and updates the viewer from time to time. The observatory shows whatever NOAA serves at the moment. The polygon files are NOAA's 2017 data (the metadata says so); the observatory reads them again only when the build is run with its refresh option.
noaa_slr.used_for: The Sea level rise layer on the 2D map and the 3D map. The residents and housing units exposed to 1 to 10 feet of sea level rise, by municipio, barrio and tract (exposure_municipio.json, exposure_barrio.json, exposure_tract.json).
noaa_slr.terms_note: NOAA's pages state no license. NOAA says the viewer shows inundation at the highest high tides and does not model storm surge, erosion, subsidence or future construction. NOAA's disclaimer says the maps show the scale of potential flooding, not exact locations, and are a planning reference that should not be used for navigation, permitting or other legal purposes, and it offers no warranty. The layers need NOAA's server to answer; the observatory shows a message when it does not. NOAA's metadata describes the method as a modified bathtub approach that accounts for tidal variation and for hydrological connectivity; the vertical accuracy depends on the elevation data and on NOAA's datum conversions; the data are a screening-level tool and are provided as is. It also says that acknowledgment of the NOAA Office for Coastal Management as the data source would be appreciated, which the credit line gives. Checked again on 2026-10-19 for the Data management page: the Digital Coast data page (https://coast.noaa.gov/digitalcoast/data/slr.html) and the metadata of the 1 to 10 ft inundation data (2017) state no license and no public-domain notice: access constraints "None", use constraints that are cautions (a screening-level tool, provided as is). So the class stays unstated; NOAA would have to state the terms.

nws_nwps.name: NWS — National Water Prediction Service (flood stages of river gauges)
nws_nwps.publisher: NOAA National Weather Service (NWS), Office of Water Prediction; San Juan Weather Forecast Office
nws_nwps.credit: Source: NOAA National Weather Service, National Water Prediction Service (flood stages)
nws_nwps.access: JSON API, no key: api.water.noaa.gov/nwps/v1/gauges with a bounding box lists the gauges of Puerto Rico; /gauges/{id} gives one gauge's USGS site number and its flood categories (action, minor, moderate, major) as a stage in feet. river_gauges.py reads them at build time; the page does not ask NWS anything.
nws_nwps.cadence: NWS revises a gauge's flood stages from time to time, after a survey or a flood. The observatory reads them when it rebuilds the river file, once a month (python river_gauges.py --refresh).
nws_nwps.used_for: The flood stages in the pop-up of the River flow layer (river_gauges.geojson, field nws).
nws_nwps.terms_note: NWS says the information on its servers is in the public domain unless noted otherwise, may not be modified and then presented as official government material, and may not be used in a way that implies endorsement by NOAA or NWS (weather.gov/disclaimer, read 2026-11-12). The observatory converts the stages from feet to metres, shows the feet beside them, and says the comparison with the water's level is its own, not an official warning. Checked 2026-11-12: 118 gauges listed for Puerto Rico, 66 of the 71 river gauges of the layer with flood stages; at each, NWS's latest reading and USGS's gauge height agreed to within 0.2 ft.

nhc_hurdat2.name: NHC — HURDAT2 Atlantic hurricane database (1851-2025)

more_links.label: NHC directory of HURDAT2 files (the build reads it to find the newest file)

nhc_hurdat2.credit: Source: NOAA National Hurricane Center, Atlantic hurricane database (HURDAT2), 1851-2025
nhc_hurdat2.access: One public text file, no key: https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/hurdat/hurdat2-1851-2025-092326.txt. When the build runs with the refresh option it reads the NHC directory (https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/hurdat/) and downloads the newest file. The build keeps every storm whose track comes within 250 km of a point near the centre of the island (18.22 N, 66.45 W), with its track points.
nhc_hurdat2.cadence: NHC updates the file after each season and when it revises older seasons. The 1851-2025 file used here was updated on 23 September 2026 and includes revisions of the 1971 to 1975 seasons. The observatory reads it as retrieved on 5 October 2026 (Snapshot 2026-10). A new file is used only when FPR rebuilds the data with the refresh option.
nhc_hurdat2.used_for: Storm tracks since 1851 on the 3D map (hurricanes.json). In the 2026-10 snapshot, 157 storms in the 1851-2025 file came within 250 km of Puerto Rico; each has its track, winds and a hurricane category.
nhc_hurdat2.terms_note: NHC says information on government servers may be used freely, and that its information must not be modified and then presented as official government material. The observatory picks storms by distance and works out the Saffir-Simpson category from the highest wind recorded while the storm was within 250 km of the island's centre point. That category is the storm's strongest wind in that zone, not necessarily the wind Puerto Rico felt. Both steps are FPR's calculation, not NHC's. The Saffir-Simpson scale (linked here) rates sustained wind only; NHC notes it does not take into account storm surge, rainfall flooding or tornadoes. NHC revises past seasons from time to time.

osm.name: OpenStreetMap

more_links.label: Overpass API (public servers and fair use)

osm.credit: Data © OpenStreetMap contributors, available under the Open Database License (ODbL)
osm.access: Two routes, no key. Overpass API queries (overpass-api.de, with overpass.kumi.systems, now operated as overpass.private.coffee, as a fallback) fetch bus stops, stations, ferry terminals, taxi stands, bicycle rental, EV charging, aerodromes and public-transport route relations. The daily Geofabrik extract for Puerto Rico (download.geofabrik.de/north-america/us/puerto-rico-latest.osm.pbf) is read on a local computer to build the road graph (roads.bin) and the place-name index (gazetteer.json). Police stations (amenity=police) are read through Overpass by facilities.py, which also tries a third public Overpass server (maps.mail.ru) when the others are busy.
osm.cadence: OpenStreetMap changes all the time, and Geofabrik refreshes its Puerto Rico file daily. The observatory took the stops on 1 October 2026 and the routes and the extract on 2 October 2026, and renews them when FPR rebuilds the data (a new snapshot). A nightly update also re-reads the ATI and municipal transit feeds and tries to re-read the OpenStreetMap routes. If the Overpass servers do not answer, the observatory keeps the routes from the last full rebuild. The Overpass servers refused requests from GitHub's servers when tested on 2 October 2026, so in the 2026-10 snapshot the OpenStreetMap routes change only at a rebuild.
osm.used_for: Bus stops, stations, terminals, taxi stands, bicycle rental, EV charging and aerodromes (transport.json); públicos (shared taxi and van routes) and other routes (transit_routes.geojson); the road network for snapping and planning routes (roads.bin); and the place-name index for search (gazetteer.json); police stations (police_stations.geojson) and their count in each municipio (facility_series.json: police_stations); city halls (town_halls.geojson, amenity=townhall, read by community_assets.py on 2026-10-18); and the signalised junctions, roundabouts and pedestrian bridges counted along each bus route in the Route analysis (route_compare.json, from road_features.geojson in docs/analysis/route-analysis-2026-10/, Geofabrik extract of 2026-10-15); and the transmission lines of 230, 115 and 38 kV, simplified, with the substations counted by municipio (power_lines.geojson, read by power_lines.py on 2026-11-14). Also the roads that the distance to essentials follows, and the check of Overture's shops: OpenStreetMap's supermarkets, pharmacies, banks and fire stations that Overture or USGS lack are added (essentials_series.json, essentials_barrio.json). Also the roads and hospitals of the estimate of residents cut off from hospitals when flooded roads or poor bridges close (cutoff_series.json, cutoff_barrio.json).
osm.terms_note: OpenStreetMap's copyright page says the data may be copied, distributed, transmitted and adapted 'as long as you credit OpenStreetMap and its contributors', and that anyone who alters or builds on the data may distribute the result only under the same license. Files in the observatory built from OpenStreetMap are the OpenStreetMap parts of transport.json and transit_routes.geojson, roads.bin, gazetteer.json, police_stations.geojson, town_halls.geojson and the junction and footbridge counts of route_compare.json. Check the license text before reusing them. OpenStreetMap is edited by volunteers, so a missing stop or route may simply be unmapped.

ati_gtfs.name: Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) — GTFS open data
ati_gtfs.publisher: Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI), Government of Puerto Rico
ati_gtfs.licence: ATI open-data terms (as is, no warranty)
ati_gtfs.credit: Source: Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI), GTFS open data (Tren Urbano, AMA/Metrobús, AcuaExpreso). The PR Data Observatory is not affiliated with or sponsored by ATI
ati_gtfs.access: One public ZIP file in the GTFS format, no key: https://docs.pr.gov/files/ATI/DATOS_ABIERTOS/GTFS/PRITA_GTFS.zip.
ati_gtfs.cadence: ATI replaces the file when schedules change. On 3 October 2026 ATI's page named a 10 August 2026 version, but the feed itself is labelled 'Updated: Aug 26, 2026'. Its service dates run from 20 July 2026 to 19 July 2027. The observatory downloads it every night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time and publishes only if something changed.
ati_gtfs.used_for: Tren Urbano, AMA, Metrobús and AcuaExpreso routes, stops and timetables (transit_routes.geojson, transport.json, trips.json, trips_sa.json, trips_su.json) and the service coverage figures.
ati_gtfs.terms_note: ATI's terms say that neither ATI nor its contractors guarantee the data are fully accurate, that the data are provided 'as is', and that ATI does not guarantee they are always available or up to date. They say the agencies keep their rights over the data, that using the data gives no rights over it and that users must follow applicable laws. They also say agency logos are reserved for official use, and that an app built on the data must make clear it is not affiliated with or sponsored by ATI unless there is an explicit agreement. ATI's page says 'Nos encontramos en el desarrollo del GTFS-RT' (it is developing GTFS-RT, the real-time feed), so the observatory shows scheduled service, not live vehicle positions.

muni_gtfs.name: Municipal transit GTFS feeds (National RTAP portal)
muni_gtfs.publisher: Each municipality, through the National Rural Transit Assistance Program (National RTAP) portal (found in the Transitland Atlas registry)

more_links.label: Transitland Atlas: National RTAP feed registry

muni_gtfs.licence: No license stated in the registry or the feeds

short.es: GTFS municipales

muni_gtfs.credit: Source: the municipality that published the route (public GTFS feed on the National RTAP portal, rapid.nationalrtap.org); feed list from the Transitland Atlas (www.transit.land)
muni_gtfs.access: The build reads the Transitland Atlas registry file for the National RTAP portal (raw.githubusercontent.com/transitland/transitland-atlas, feeds/nationalrtap.org.dmfr.json), picks the Puerto Rico municipal feeds, and downloads each feed's ZIP from rapid.nationalrtap.org. No key. On 3 October 2026 the registry listed 24 Puerto Rico municipal feeds.
muni_gtfs.cadence: Each municipality updates its own feed when it chooses. The observatory re-reads the registry and every feed each night at 04:17 Puerto Rico time, so a new or updated feed appears the next day. On 2 October 2026 the 24 municipal feeds were 16 current, 1 expiring and 7 expired (end date passed).
muni_gtfs.used_for: Municipal bus and trolley routes, stops and timetables (transit_routes.geojson, transport.json, trips.json, trips_sa.json, trips_su.json) and the service coverage figures.
muni_gtfs.terms_note: The registry and the feed files state no license. FTA's National Transit Database rules, from report year 2023, require reporters with fixed-route service to keep a public-domain GTFS dataset. That is an FTA requirement, not a license printed on each municipal feed. Check each municipality's terms before reusing a feed beyond viewing it. The portal page names no publisher or license; it is attributed to National RTAP by its domain and by the Transitland registry file name. Feed addresses are found through the Transitland Atlas (CC BY 4.0), which asks users to link to its repository or to www.transit.land. Quality varies: many feeds have no route shapes (the observatory draws those routes along roads), some list stops out of travel order, and some have expired.

ntd.name: FTA — National Transit Database, Puerto Rico reporters
ntd.publisher: Federal Transit Administration (FTA); this copy of the list is kept by the Transitland Atlas project

more_links.label: NTD GTFS weblinks, report year 2023, on Data.gov

ntd.licence: US Government works (FTA); Transitland Atlas registry: CC BY 4.0
ntd.credit: Source: Federal Transit Administration (FTA), National Transit Database (2023 GTFS weblinks), via the Transitland Atlas, www.transit.land
ntd.access: One public CSV file on GitHub, no key: raw.githubusercontent.com/transitland/transitland-atlas/main/external-data-for-reference/ntd-gtfs-weblinks/2023-gtfs-weblinks.csv, a copy of the FTA list.
ntd.cadence: FTA releases the list by report year and says an up-to-date list is refreshed monthly. The observatory reads the report-year 2023 copy, and re-reads it each night and when FPR rebuilds the data (a new snapshot).
ntd.used_for: The checklist of Puerto Rico transit agencies that report to FTA. On 2 October 2026 the observatory kept 39 of them: 36 municipal systems, AMA, the maritime transport authority and the públicos authority. The Operators list adds ATI, three municipalities that publish feeds but are not on the checklist, and the OpenStreetMap routes (44 entries in the 2026-10 snapshot). The checklist also feeds the fields that say whether a municipality has a system.
ntd.terms_note: The Transitland Atlas repository is licensed CC BY 4.0, and its README asks users to link to the repository or to www.transit.land. A listing here shows that an agency reports to FTA, not that it publishes a public feed. For operators with no feed, the Weblink column of the FTA list is copied into operators.json as the feed link (one operator in the 2026-10 snapshot). It points to a web page, not to a GTFS feed. A link into a person's own cloud storage is not published.

faa_airports.name: FAA airports (BTS National Transportation Atlas Database)
faa_airports.publisher: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), distributed by the Bureau of Transportation Statistics (BTS) National Transportation Atlas Database (NTAD)

more_links.label: NTAD service the build reads, Aviation Facilities (layer 0)

faa_airports.licence: US Government work (not copyrighted; unrestricted public use)
faa_airports.credit: Source: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and Bureau of Transportation Statistics (BTS), National Transportation Atlas Database
faa_airports.access: ArcGIS REST layer (a public web service) on services.arcgis.com (/xOi1kZaI0eWDREZv/arcgis/rest/services/NTAD_Aviation_Facilities/FeatureServer/0), queried with STATE_CODE='PR' and SITE_TYPE_CODE='A' (airports; heliports and other site types are left out) for name, city, use, ownership, airport ID, status, effective date and coordinates. No key. The build code was changed on 5 October 2026 because the older geo.dot.gov address (Hosted/Airports_) no longer answered; the published transport.json was built before that change.
faa_airports.cadence: NTAD updates the aviation facilities every 28 days from FAA data. The observatory keeps one snapshot, downloaded on 1 October 2026 (14 Puerto Rico airports), and renews it only when FPR rebuilds the data (a new snapshot).
faa_airports.used_for: The list of Puerto Rico airports (14 in the 2026-10 snapshot), whether each is open to public use, and the airport counts per municipality (transport.json, municipalities.json); and the Airports and heliports map layer (airports.geojson, transport_inventories.py), which reads every facility type and draws the facilities open to public use or owned by a public body.
faa_airports.terms_note: The observatory treats the FAA list as the official airport list and drops OpenStreetMap aerodromes within 2 km of an FAA airport. Helipads and other small airfields come from OpenStreetMap. The service the build now reads (services.arcgis.com, linked here) holds more facility types (44 Puerto Rico facilities in October 2026), so the build keeps only site type A (airports). That query returns 15 airports on 5 October 2026, one more than the 14 in the published 2026-10 snapshot; the extra one shows after the next full build. Counts of all facilities are not comparable with the observatory's airport list.

uber.name: Uber — cities served in Puerto Rico (service listing)
uber.licence: Public web page; no license stated

short.es: listado de servicio de Uber

uber.credit: Source: Uber, cities served in Puerto Rico (uber.com), checked 1 October 2026; listed or not listed only
uber.access: FPR read Uber's page and typed the municipality names it lists into the observatory by hand (57 names, checked 1 October 2026). The observatory does not call Uber's servers.
uber.cadence: Uber can change its page at any time. The observatory's list is a dated snapshot that FPR updates by hand.
uber.used_for: The 'listed on Uber's cities page' yes or no for each municipality (municipalities.json) and the ride-hailing note in the Transit tab.
uber.terms_note: The page lists towns and neighbourhoods and says Uber's service reaches beyond the places listed, so 'not listed' does not mean Uber does not operate there. Only a yes or no per municipality is recorded; the observatory copies nothing else from the page. On 4 October 2026 the page linked 167 places. Counted by the municipality named in each link's address, the page lists places in 58 of the 78 municipios. The observatory's list, checked on 1 October 2026, has 57 names. On 4 October 2026 the page also listed Maunabo, which the observatory shows as not listed.

jp_put2015.name: Junta de Planificación — Land Use Plan (PUT 2015)
jp_put2015.publisher: Junta de Planificación de Puerto Rico (Government of Puerto Rico)

more_links.label: Public copy of the layer on ArcGIS Online

short.en: Junta de Planificación land use plan (PUT 2015)
short.es: Plan de Uso de Terrenos 2015 de la Junta de Planificación

jp_put2015.credit: Source: Junta de Planificación de Puerto Rico, Plan de Uso de Terrenos (Land Use Plan, PUT 2015)
jp_put2015.access: The observatory uses a copy of the Junta's official shapefile (a standard map-data file), in the version of 30 November 2015, converted to the WGS 84 coordinate system. The Junta's page links the map and the memorial as PDFs but offers no shapefile, so it gives no download link for the file the observatory uses. If the observatory's copy is missing, the build reads a public copy on ArcGIS Online (services6.arcgis.com, Puerto_Rico_Land_Use_Plan, layer 0), which shows no owner or license text and was last edited on 24 January 2019.
jp_put2015.cadence: The plan has a ten-year term (the Junta's page); the observatory's shapefile is the 30 November 2015 version. The Junta's page lists a review process for a new plan (PUT-2025). The observatory uses the 2015 version and does not refresh it.
jp_put2015.used_for: The land-use classes drawn on the maps (landuse.geojson), the land class of each tourism place, and each municipality's share of urban, urbanizable, rustic and protected land.
jp_put2015.terms_note: The Junta's page footer carries a general website notice ('© 2022 Puerto Rico Innovation & Technology Service. Todos los derechos reservados', meaning all rights reserved) that does not mention the land-use data. The plan classifies land. Zoning districts are in each municipality's territorial plan. The maps draw outlines simplified by up to about 100 metres; the statistics use the full shapes. The 2015 plan may be replaced by the review the Junta lists.

fpr_housing_2023.name: The State of Housing in Puerto Rico (FPR, 2023)

short.es: estudio de FPR de 2023 sobre la vivienda

fpr_housing_2023.credit: Source: Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR), The State of Housing in Puerto Rico (2023); funded in part by the Equitable Neighborhood Development program of NALCAB (National Association of Latino Community Asset Builders)
fpr_housing_2023.access: The study's published figures (the LIHTC projects and the headline figures) were typed by hand into the observatory and are published in housing.json. The observatory does not read the PDF.
fpr_housing_2023.cadence: Published in May 2023 (the PDF is dated 12 May 2023) and never updated. The observatory reproduces the figures as published.
fpr_housing_2023.used_for: The study's own figures, kept as published, on the Housing page and in housing.json: the LIHTC projects funded with CDBG-DR and the headline housing figures.
fpr_housing_2023.terms_note: The study's full title is 'The State of Housing in Puerto Rico: An Analysis of the Factors That Impact Housing and Rent Prices in Puerto Rico and Proposed Strategies to Increase Housing Affordability'. The study names the US Census among its sources, and describes the LIHTC projects as provided by the CDBG-DR portal; the LIHTC table in the PDF is an image with no readable source line. The observatory shows that table as published in 2023. FPR has not compared it with the federal source, and it is not refreshed from HUD's current LIHTC database. The PDF carries no license line, and FPR's website footer reads '© Foundation for Puerto Rico'. The Housing page numbers some tables differently from the PDF at this link, which numbers the LIHTC table 12. Cite a table by its title and the PDF's number.

fpr_method.name: FPR affordability method (State of Housing 2023, Table 8)
fpr_method.publisher: Foundation for Puerto Rico (method); US Census Bureau (input data)
fpr_method.licence: FPR method; inputs are US Census Bureau ACS estimates
fpr_method.credit: Source: Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) calculation on US Census Bureau American Community Survey 5-year estimates, following The State of Housing in Puerto Rico (2023), Table 8
fpr_method.access: Calculated by the build from ACS tables: B19013 (median household income) and B25077 (median home value) for the affordability figures, and B25070 and B25091 for the study-style cost-burden distributions. There is no separate download.
fpr_method.cadence: Recalculated whenever the ACS figures are rebuilt, each time FPR rebuilds the data (a new snapshot). The method constants never change, so years differ only through incomes and prices.
fpr_method.used_for: The maximum affordable 30-year loan and the home ownership affordability ratio, by municipality and year.
fpr_method.terms_note: The method: 30 percent of income goes to housing, about 78 percent of that (430/549) to principal and interest, on a 30-year loan at a fixed 5 percent rate. FPR inferred the 5 percent rate from the study's published Puerto Rico example, so it is a modelling assumption, not the market rate of any particular year. The Housing page calls this method 'Table 6'. In the PDF at this link, Table 6 is the rent-burden table (Gross Rent as a Percentage of Household Income) and the Home Ownership Affordability Ratio is Table 8, so cite Table 8. The result is an indicator, not a loan limit and not advice on buying a home.

openfreemap.name: OpenFreeMap vector tiles (base map of every map)

more_links.label: OpenFreeMap Quick Start (Leaflet through MapLibre GL Leaflet)
Liberty style used by the 3D map
Positron style used by the 2D map and the WCRP maps
Bright, Dark and Fiord styles, offered in the 'Base map' choice

openfreemap.licence: Free public instance with no key, no request limit and no SLA, provided as is; map data from OpenStreetMap (ODbL), schema by OpenMapTiles
openfreemap.access: Vector tiles in the OpenMapTiles schema, with a style, fonts and icons, streamed live from tiles.openfreemap.org to each visitor's browser: the 'liberty' style (https://tiles.openfreemap.org/styles/liberty) on the 3D map, drawn by MapLibre GL JS, and the 'positron' style (https://tiles.openfreemap.org/styles/positron) on the 2D map and the two WCRP maps; on the 2D and 3D maps a 'Base map' choice also offers its 'bright', 'dark' and 'fiord' styles (https://tiles.openfreemap.org/styles/bright, /dark, /fiord), three USGS maps (a separate source) or no base map, and a style is fetched only when it is shown. The 2D and WCRP maps are drawn by MapLibre GL JS under Leaflet through MapLibre GL Leaflet once each page is ready. No key or sign-up. The observatory stores no tiles. Every style and credit line is set in one file, site/js/core/basemap.js.
openfreemap.cadence: OpenFreeMap says it offers full planet downloads every week. Its homepage and terms do not say how often the live map tiles refresh. The observatory does nothing to refresh them.
openfreemap.used_for: The base map under every map: the 2D map (index.html), the two WCRP maps (wcrp.html) and the 3D map (3d.html), where its building shapes are also raised in 3D.
openfreemap.terms_note: OpenFreeMap's homepage (read 2026-10-23) says attribution is required, asks for 'OpenFreeMap © OpenMapTiles Data from OpenStreetMap' (crediting OpenFreeMap itself is optional), and says the public instance has no limit on map views or requests and no SLA. Its terms (last updated 2026-10-14) say the service is provided as is, with no warranty, may end at any time without notice, forbid automated collection other than small offline downloads (at most 3,000 tiles or 50 MB, 4 parallel requests, a unique User-Agent), and are governed by Hungarian law with arbitration in Budapest. Each tile request goes through Cloudflare to OpenFreeMap's servers and sends the visitor's IP address. When the service does not answer, the observatory's maps show their data on a plain background and say so; they never fall back to the OpenStreetMap Foundation's own tile servers.

usgs_basemaps.name: USGS National Map base maps (aerial imagery, topographic, shaded relief)

USGS Shaded Relief base map service

usgs_basemaps.credit: Base map: U.S. Geological Survey, National Geospatial Program; on the aerial imagery also 'Orthoimagery: USDA, USGS' (the service's own copyright line)
usgs_basemaps.access: Raster tiles (256 px, JPEG or PNG) streamed live from basemap.nationalmap.gov to each visitor's browser, only when a viewer picks one of these maps in the 'Base map' choice of the 2D map or the 3D view: 'Aerial imagery' (USGSImageryOnly), 'Topographic' (USGSTopo) and 'Shaded relief' (USGSShadedReliefOnly), each to zoom 16 and enlarged above it. The style is built in site/js/core/basemap.js; no key or sign-up. The observatory stores no tiles.
usgs_basemaps.cadence: Each service states its own refresh: Imagery Only 'Data refreshed June, 2024', Topo 'Data refreshed September 4, 2026', Shaded Relief 'Data refreshed September, 2025' (read 2026-11-13). The capture dates of the photographs vary by area and are not given per tile. The observatory does nothing to refresh them.
usgs_basemaps.used_for: Three choices of the 'Base map' switcher on the 2D map (index.html) and the 3D view (3d.html), where they are draped over the terrain.

USGS-authored data are in the U.S. public domain. The USGS Imagery Topo service (imagery with labels) retires on 2026-11-16, so it is not offered. These are pictures: they hold no OpenStreetMap data, the map inspector cannot read them, and the 3D view draws no OpenStreetMap buildings over them. Each tile request goes to the USGS's servers and sends the visitor's IP address. When the tiles do not answer, the maps show their data on a plain background and say so.

aws_terrain.licence: Mapzen terrain tiles: attribution required (see Mapzen's attribution page)

aws_terrain.used_for: The 3D terrain and hillshade on the 3D map (3d.html).

It lists 3DEP, GMTED2010 and SRTM (courtesy of the U.S. Geological Survey) for the United States and ETOPO1 (NOAA) for the globe. It does not say which dataset fills each tile around Puerto Rico, so the credit line names all of them. The AWS registry asks users to state the access date and the registry address. nominatim.name: OpenStreetMap Nominatim (optional address lookup)
nominatim.licence: Data under the ODbL; the OpenStreetMap Foundation's usage policy applies
nominatim.access: Only when a visitor clicks 'Look up as an address online', the page sends the typed text from the visitor's browser to nominatim.openstreetmap.org/search. The request asks for up to 6 results (format jsonv2, country code pr) inside a box around the island. Nothing is sent while the visitor types. No key. Nothing is stored.
nominatim.cadence: Each lookup is live, so it reflects OpenStreetMap at that moment. The observatory keeps no copy.
nominatim.used_for: The optional address lookup in the search boxes and the route planner, used when the observatory's own place index has no match.
nominatim.terms_note: The usage policy allows at most one request per second, forbids search-as-you-type, asks for a valid Referer or User-Agent and visible attribution, and lets the Foundation block heavy use. The observatory calls Nominatim only on a click. The text typed goes to OpenStreetMap's servers with the visitor's IP address.

leaflet.name: Leaflet 1.9.4 and Leaflet.markercluster 1.5.3

noaa_slr_scenarios.name: NOAA — Sea level rise scenarios (2022 report)
noaa_slr_scenarios.publisher: NOAA National Ocean Service, with partner agencies

short.es: escenarios de aumento del nivel del mar de NOAA (2022)

noaa_slr_scenarios.credit: Adapted from: Sweet, W.V., et al., 2022: Global and Regional Sea Level Rise Scenarios for the United States. NOAA Technical Report NOS 01. Values approximated by Foundation for Puerto Rico
noaa_slr_scenarios.access: No file is downloaded. FPR typed approximate values into the 3D map. They give global mean sea level in metres above the year-2000 level for four scenarios (Intermediate-Low, Intermediate, Intermediate-High and High) at 2020, 2050, 2100 and 2150. Values between those years are interpolated in a straight line.
noaa_slr_scenarios.cadence: NOAA issued the report in 2022, its first update since 2017. The observatory's numbers change only when FPR updates them by hand.
noaa_slr_scenarios.used_for: The Years clock on the 3D map: a year and a scenario give a rise in feet, which picks the nearest layer (1 to 10 feet) from NOAA's Sea Level Rise Viewer.
noaa_slr_scenarios.terms_note: The values are approximations of the report's global mean sea level tables. The 2100 values match the report, but some others differ: the 2050 Intermediate-Low value (0.24 m) is the report's observation-based extrapolation, not the scenario (0.20 m); the 2050 Intermediate (0.30 m) and High (0.44 m) values are 0.02 m and 0.01 m above the report (0.28 m and 0.43 m); the 2020 Intermediate-High and High values (0.07 m) are 0.01 m below the report (0.08 m); and the 2150 Intermediate-High and High values (2.9 m and 3.9 m) are 0.2 m above the report (2.7 m and 3.7 m). The values are global averages, not values for Puerto Rico's coast. The result is indicative, not a forecast. The report defines five scenarios (Low to High) and the observatory offers four, without Low. The report's notice says that use of its information for publicity or advertising of proprietary products or their tests is not authorized. Checked again on 2026-10-19 for the Data management page: the report states no license and no public-domain notice, and its notice restricts one use (publicity or advertising of proprietary products), so the class stays unstated.

github_pages.name: GitHub Pages and Actions (hosting, nightly refresh)
github_pages.licence: Service terms, not a data license
github_pages.access: A workflow (GitHub Actions) publishes the site folder to GitHub Pages each time the site files change on the main branch and after each nightly refresh that changes data. github_pages.cadence: Republished when the site files change and after each nightly refresh that changes data.
github_pages.used_for: Serving every page and data file of the observatory, running the nightly transit refresh, and the optional GitHub issue link in the chat.
github_pages.terms_note: This is a hosting service, not a data license. GitHub's Pages limits page says published sites may be no larger than 1 GB, with soft limits of 100 GB of bandwidth a month and 10 builds an hour (the build limit does not apply to custom workflows). Like any web host, GitHub receives the visitor's IP address when a page loads; see GitHub's privacy statement.

jp_comunidades_especiales.publisher: Junta de Planificación de Puerto Rico (Government of Puerto Rico)

jp_comunidades_especiales.credit: Source: Junta de Planificación de Puerto Rico, delimitation of the Comunidades Especiales (Ley 1-2001), 2006
jp_comunidades_especiales.access: The build reads a public copy of the Junta's layer on ArcGIS Online (services6.arcgis.com, Comunidades_Especiales, layer 0), held by the same account as the copy of the Land Use Plan the observatory uses. jp_comunidades_especiales.used_for: The Comunidades Especiales outlines on the 2D map (comunidades.geojson) and the name, place, housing units, community type and reported hazards shown when you click one.

fpr_wcrp.name: FPR — Whole Community Resilience Planning (WCRP) program, list of communities
fpr_wcrp.credit: Source: Foundation for Puerto Rico, Whole Community Resilience Planning (WCRP) program, list of communities and program tracker as of 2026-10-06
fpr_wcrp.access: FPR's WCRP document index (WCRP-RAG, list_comunidades) lists each community with its municipality, WCRP region, plan status and subrecipient; FPR copied that list into wcrp_comunidades.csv on 2026-10-06. Seven communities in phase 1 have no documents in that index yet, so their rows come from FPR's Smartsheet tracker of the program (TRACKER_Planning Phases, 79 communities) and their municipality from their work plans. Both sources are internal; the observatory publishes seven columns (community, plan status, municipality, the place the point was set from, region, subrecipient and how the point was placed) and an approximate point.
fpr_wcrp.cadence: Copied once, on 2026-10-06. Nothing refreshes it automatically: FPR adds or updates rows in the CSV by hand and runs wcrp.py.

nhc_slosh.name: NHC — SLOSH storm surge maps for Puerto Rico (Maximum of MEOWs, category 1 to 5, high tide)
nhc_slosh.publisher: NOAA National Hurricane Center (NHC), Storm Surge Unit

more_links.label: Puerto Rico maps the observatory reads (PR_SLOSH_MOM_Inundation.zip, 7.3 MB)
About SLOSH and the MOM product

nhc_slosh.credit: Source: NOAA National Hurricane Center, SLOSH Maximum of MEOWs storm surge maps for Puerto Rico (2018)
nhc_slosh.access: One public ZIP file, no key: https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/gis/hazardmaps/PR_SLOSH_MOM_Inundation.zip (7.3 MB, dated 30 November 2018). It holds five GeoTIFFs, one per hurricane category, of about 10 m cells in NAD83, each cell coded by the depth of water above ground in 1 ft bands (1 = under 1 ft, 2 = 1 to 2 ft, and so on). exposure.py downloads it once, reads the cell under each 2020 Census block's internal point with the project's own GeoTIFF reader (raster.py), and keeps only the counts of residents and housing units of each area, not the maps.
nhc_slosh.cadence: NHC published the Puerto Rico maps in November 2018 (the files inside are dated November 2017) and has not replaced them since; the mainland maps were updated later (version 4). The freshness check watches the ZIP file's date and size. A new file is used only when FPR rebuilds the exposure series with the refresh option.
nhc_slosh.used_for: The residents and housing units in the area that NOAA's storm surge maps show flooded by a category 1 to 5 hurricane, at any depth and under 3 ft of water or more, by municipio, barrio and census tract (exposure_municipio.json, exposure_barrio.json, exposure_tract.json; families surge_cat1 to surge_cat5 and surge_deep_cat1 to surge_deep_cat5).
nhc_slosh.terms_note: NHC says information on government servers may be used freely and is in the public domain, and that it must not be modified and then presented as official government material. The map metadata say the data show the scale of potential flooding, not the exact location, for general awareness of the storm surge hazard at a city or community level, not for a parcel or grid cell; they do not account for erosion, subsidence or future construction, and the risk may extend beyond the SLOSH model's grids. They are a planning reference and storm surge awareness tool, not for navigation, permitting, legal or regulatory purposes. Each map is the Maximum of MEOWs (MOM): for each category, the highest water among many hypothetical storms of different tracks, speeds and sizes, at high tide, so it is a near worst case, not one storm. The maps are not evacuation zones; those are set by Puerto Rico's emergency management bureau.

K is required only on Sample Panel sections, and the Field Manual says statewide or system-wide values shall not be used. For 764 of the 1,582 junctions (48%) the road has no K and the observatory used the median K of its functional class (k_imputed): the observatory's own estimate, which HPMS guidance does not endorse. AADT is an annual average of both directions; AADT x K is a design-hour volume (one of the busiest hours of the year), not a typical weekday peak, and says nothing about speed or delay. The NTAD item advises against comparing states on the sampled items; only Puerto Rico is used.
